rendered: The review does not really recommend tens of nanometres. Its recommendation is for thinner films: the coating thickness should be below ten nanometers[1] for better electrochemical performance. A summary in the outlook makes the same point, saying the maximum thickness of the widely used, low-diffusivity coating materials is thicknesses are usually recommend to around ∼10 nm[2]. The reasoning is about ionic transport through the coating. The review notes that the lithium-ion diffusivity of the most oxides and fluorides is extremely low, particularly for ZrO2[3]. Taking the diffusion time as the square of the diffusion length divided by the diffusivity, and varying the diffusion length from 5nm to 50nm[4], longer diffusion times appear for thicker layers, and the measured performance appears to be ited by the ionic diffusion at the coating layer[5]. So for these low-diffusivity oxides, a thin layer keeps lithium transport through the coating from becoming the bottleneck. The tens-of-nanometre thicknesses seen in the literature are described as a practical outcome rather than the target: they are tens of nanometers as it is difficult to be controlled by easily scalable[6] processes. A further caution is that ZrO2 can react with lithium to form secondary phases such as Li2ZrO3[7], which causes capacity fading.
